sous_titre: From Stone Age hunters to longships, from stave churches to fjords: ten thousand years of Norwegian heritage.
intro: Norway is not just a landscape of fjords and the Northern Lights: it is a country shaped by the sea, the mountains and the ice, where every valley has preserved its farms, churches and graves. This account traces, period by period, how this territory on the edge of Europe became a nation — from the rock art of Alta to the Norway of oil and World Heritage sites.

chapitres.texte: As soon as the glaciers retreated, some 11,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers followed game and fish along the coastlines revealed by the melting ice. They left behind one of the richest collections of rock art in Europe: at Alta, in the far north, thousands of engravings dating from 5,000 to 2,000 BC depict reindeer, bears, boats and hunting scenes — a site recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. These images are not mere drawings: they depict a world in which humans, animals and the spirit interact.

chapitres.titre: Bronze, iron and the first leaders
chapitres.texte: During the Bronze Age (1700–500 BC), engravings of ships and sun discs began to appear on the rocks in the south: the sea and the sun were already central to local beliefs. During the Iron Age, the landscape became dotted with farms, burial mounds and the first hilltop fortifications (bygdeborg). Local chieftains grew wealthy from the fur trade, iron from the marshes and whetstones. The society that would give rise to the Vikings was already in place: hierarchical, warlike and looking out to sea.

chapitres.titre: The Viking Age: from the farm to Valhalla
chapitres.texte: Around 793, the Scandinavians appeared on the seas of Europe. But before the raids, there was everyday life: people were born in the longhouse on the farm (like the large chieftain’s hall reconstructed at Borg in the Lofoten Islands), one grew up amongst the mountain pastures (seter) and the fields, and justice was administered at the thing, the assembly of free men. Merchants and craftsmen bustled about in trading centres such as Kaupang; Avaldsnes, on the Nordvegen sea route — ‘the Northern Way’, which gave the country its name — is a royal seat. Then came the ships: the Gokstad drakkar and the Oseberg drakkar, masterpieces now preserved in Oslo. And at the end of the journey, death: the great royal burial mounds of Borre, Oseberg, Gjellestad and Herlaugshaugen — now nominated for World Heritage status — were believed to guide the deceased to Valhalla. It is this entire journey that our ‘Viking Trail’ tour retraces.

In the 10th and 11th centuries, kings such as Olav Tryggvason and later Olav Haraldsson — the future Saint Olav, who died at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030 — imposed Christianity. This gave rise to a masterpiece unique in the world: the stavkirke, or stave church, with its portals carved with dragons, where paganism survived alongside the cross. Of nearly a thousand such structures, around thirty remain — Urnes (a World Heritage Site), Borgund, Heddal — black, tiered silhouettes like drakkars turned skywards. Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim became the great pilgrimage site of the North.

chapitres.titre: Bergen, the Hanseatic League and the sea
chapitres.texte: In the Middle Ages, Norway’s economy was based on the sea: stockfisch (dried cod) from the Lofoten Islands was traded throughout Europe. Bergen became a major trading post of the Hanseatic League; its wooden quays, Bryggen, which have been burnt down and rebuilt identically since the 14th century, are now a World Heritage Site. The Black Death of 1349 decimated the country and left it weakened. In 1397, the Kalmar Union placed Norway under the Danish crown — a union that was to last for more than four centuries.

Four ‘Danish’ centuries (1380–1814) left their mark: administration, the written language, and towns rebuilt after fires. Røros, a copper-mining town with its blackened wooden houses, is a World Heritage Site. In 1814, in the wake of the Napoleonic Wars, Norway adopted a Constitution at Eidsvoll — on 17 May, which remains a national holiday — but was immediately ceded to Sweden. This marked the beginning of a long 19th century of national self-assertion.

The 19th century in Norway was a time of identity-seeking and self-assertion: Ibsen in theatre, Grieg in music, Munch in painting, and the folktale collectors Asbjørnsen and Moe, who immortalised the trolls and huldres of folklore. The language itself split into two forms: Bokmål, derived from Danish, and Nynorsk, reconstructed by Ivar Aasen from rural dialects. In 1905, Norway peacefully severed its union with Sweden and chose a king for itself: it was once again independent.

Geography is a heritage in its own right. The western fjords — Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord, both World Heritage Sites — are glacial valleys flooded by the sea, lined with farms clinging to the slopes and waterfalls. The coastline, stretching over 100,000 km including its islands, has long depended on fishing and coastal shipping: fishing villages with red huts (rorbuer) in the Lofoten Islands, isolated lighthouses (fyr) guarding the straits, and shipyards. Here, the sea is not an obstacle but a route.

chapitres.titre: Farms, mountain pastures and rural life
chapitres.texte: In the valleys and mountains, the farm (gård) is at the heart of Norwegian society. In summer, livestock were taken up to the mountain pastures (seter), where small huts were used to make butter and cheese — a pastoral system still evident in the landscape through thousands of such sites. Granaries on stilts (stabbur), mills and water-powered sawmills (sagbruk) bear witness to the tenacious self-sufficiency of the farming community, where wood reigns supreme and every carved object bears the mark of the craftsman’s hand.

In the north, in a region that transcends borders and stretches into Sweden, Finland and Russia, live the indigenous Sámi people (Sápmi). As reindeer herders and joik singers, the Sámi have their own language, their own crafts (duodji) and a history long marked by forced ‘Norwegianisation’. Their sites — places of sacrifice, camps and graves — form a unique heritage that this edition highlights in a dedicated feature. To recognise Sápmi is to recognise that there are many ways of being Norwegian.

chapitres.titre: Industry, hydroelectric power and modern Norway
chapitres.texte: At the end of the 19th century, hydropower transformed the country: waterfalls were harnessed to generate electricity, and with them came the rise of industrial towns such as Rjukan and Notodden – now listed as World Heritage Sites for their industrial heritage – producing aluminium, fertiliser and paper. After 1969, oil and gas from the North Sea made Norway one of the world’s most prosperous countries. But the nation remains attached to its farms, wooden churches and fjords — a heritage it protects and shares, and which this app invites you to explore, one map at a time.
